prime.problem: "The model is slow" is not something you can fix. Without a breakdown you tune the wrong thing: you buy hardware when the answer was 20× too long, or switch hosts when the wait was all hidden thinking.
prime.fits: This is the map for the whole course. Every later card is one term of a single formula: a start (time to first token), plus tokens ÷ speed, repeated for every call. The agents overview then wraps that formula in a loop.
expect: fewer tokens vs faster tokens vs a shorter start
prime.goal: Place every card in the course on one causal map, and say which term of the formula a given change attacks and roughly how big the win can be.

attend: Which term of the formula is a multiply and which only adds seconds, and why does that decide the ranking of levers?
Why do thinking tokens show up in two places at once (the start and the writing time)?
For the 653-token FizzBuzz run, what fraction of the 42 s is the start? What would have to change for the start to dominate instead?
Why does the ranking put "change host" above "buy hardware" but below "cut tokens"?
Why is caching's 83× speed-up not an 83× faster response?

must: Tokens are written one at a time at a fixed pace → writing time = tokens ÷ output speed → for any answer longer than a few sentences the multiply dwarfs the start → cut tokens first

Each lever touches exactly one term → fewer tokens (thinking, length, calls), faster tokens (host, hardware, quantization, speculative decoding), or a shorter start (caching, cold start, network) → name the term before picking the fix
Thinking is output that is hidden → it delays the first visible token and is paid at the same per-token speed → effort settings move both TTFT and total time (16–23× in the measurements)
An agent repeats the formula N times → per-call costs multiply by the call count → the number of calls is itself a token lever you choose when you pick the tool
elevated: Grey rows (cold start, network + queue) add or remove seconds rather than scale with tokens → they matter only when the answer is short
reference: the exact speed-up per lever row (36×, 3.1×, 2.5×, 83×)

compress.prompt: Close the card and draw the course's causal map: knobs on the left (prompt settings, thinking effort, model, host, harness), the four metrics in the middle, end-to-end time on the right, with one arrow per knob. Then write the formula from memory and circle the term each of the 13 cards explains.
checklist: TTFT = network + queue + cold start + prefill (and hidden thinking for reasoning models)
writing time = (thinking + answer tokens) ÷ output speed
the whole bracket repeats per call, plus tool time between calls
levers group into fewer tokens, faster tokens, shorter start
cut tokens first, pick the host second, buy hardware last
the real target is time to a correct result, not raw speed

retrieve.q: Explain why cutting output tokens usually beats buying a faster chip, using the formula rather than examples.
answer: tokens sit in the numerator of the writing-time term, speed in the denominator
you control token count for free (prompt, max_tokens, thinking off); speed needs money or a host change
measured: 653 → 82 tokens was about 7.9×; M3 → M3 Max is about 3.1×

retrieve.q: Walk the FizzBuzz request through the formula term by term on the M3 with thinking off (N = 1, 653 tokens, 15.4 t/s, warm).
answer: network ≈ 0.3 ms locally, queue 0, cold start 0 when warm
prefill of a short prompt: about 0.1–0.3 s
so almost all of the time is the multiply, not the start

retrieve.q: A user's hosted chat feels slow. Give one situation where prompt caching is the right lever and one where it is nearly useless, and say which term each case is dominated by.
answer: right: a long, stable prefix re-sent each turn (TTFT dominated by prefill)
useless: a short prompt with a long answer (writing time dominates)
caching only shrinks t<sub>prefill</sub>, never tokens ÷ speed

compare.q: This card's formula ends at the total time for one attempt; the agents overview divides by a success probability. What does that extra denominator capture that no lever here can, and when does it flip the ranking of levers?
answer: here every attempt is assumed to succeed; there a wrong result means repeating the work
checks raise p<sup>N</sup>, which no speed lever touches
on a multi-step task a slower, checked or careful setup can reach a correct result sooner (83.5 s vs 37.9 s example)

compare.q: Both describe latency with TTFT and per-token speed. What changes when the viewpoint moves from one user's request to a server handling many users?
answer: this card: one request's wait; serving view adds throughput across users
batching raises total throughput but lowers each user's speed
a host's measured output speed already includes how much it shares the chip

predict.q: Suppose a new host serves the same model 10× faster per token but has 3 s more TTFT. For which answer lengths (on a baseline of 66 t/s and 1.39 s TTFT) is it actually faster end to end? Commit to a rough cut-off before revealing.
predict.answer: The new host saves n ÷ 66 − n ÷ 660 = n × 0.0136 s and costs 3 s extra. It wins once n × 0.0136 > 3, so beyond about 220 tokens. Short answers (a few sentences) are faster on the old host; anything code-sized is faster on the new one. That's the start-vs-multiply split in one line.

apply.task: Pick one real request you make often (a chat question, a code edit in an agent, a local Ollama call). Estimate each term of the formula: N, TTFT parts, thinking tokens, answer tokens, speed and tool time. Then name the single lever from the ranking that would cut the total most, and estimate the new total.
apply.done: You have a filled-in formula with a number for every term, one chosen lever, and a before/after estimate. The lever attacks the largest term.
apply.hint: On a local model with ollama run --verbose you get load duration, prompt eval and eval rate directly. On a hosted model, use Artificial Analysis medians for TTFT and speed, and count tokens from the usage field.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the cut-off length where a faster-per-token host wins?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why caching's 83× doesn't make the whole response 83× faster?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: effort setting → thinking tokens, or thinking tokens → delayed first token?
Which lever did you assume mattered most before reading, and where did it land in the ranking?
Which card will you read first to repair the weakest term in your own formula?
